findings.finding: Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for distinct a+b+c=n. Small n shows pattern: best triples often include 1,2 or 2,4,6 etc. For huge n, optimal is to take three numbers sharing a large common factor d (≈n/3) so LCM≈d·k where k is minimal lcm of three distinct numbers summing to n/d (≤6). Thus f(n)≈n/3·L where L∈{4,6,8,10,12,…} depending on n mod small base. Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025!; since M=3^{2025!} huge, f(M+c)≈M·L/3, floor gives L/3 (integer). So each g(c) equals L/3. Find L for each N=M+c via n mod 6,8,…; sum six values → rational p/q. Finally compute (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure distinctness, handle cases where n small relative to d, verify L/3 integer.

Insights: f(n)=min X with three distinct divisors summing to n ⇔ ∃ distinct a,b∈D(X) s.t. a+b=n−X. Hence X must satisfy n−X ≤ max (a+b) = largest two proper divisors of X. For X even, max (a+b)=X/2+X/3≈5/6 X, so n≤11/6 X ⇒ X≥6n/11. For n≈M=3^{2025!}, the minimal X is the smallest integer ≥6n/11 whose two largest proper divisors can sum to n−X. For M (power of 3) the two largest proper divisors are M/3 and M/9, giving max (a+b)=4/9 M; thus X=M works only if c=n−M is sum of two powers of 3. Otherwise the minimal X is the next integer ≥6n/11 that meets the divisor‑sum condition. Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025!; since 2025!≪M, g(c)=⌊2025!·(f(M+c)/M)⌋/2025! = (⌊2025!·r⌋)/2025! where r≈f/M. Sum the six g’s, reduce to p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Key pitfall: assuming f=n or f=M; must use bound X≥6n/11 and check two‑largest‑divisor condition. Use that for each given c.

Insights: f(n)=min N with n−N = sum of two distinct proper divisors of N. Hence N>n/2. For n=M+c (M=3^{2025!}) we need N≈αM (½<α≤1). g(c)=⌊2025!·α⌋/2025!; since 2025! divisible by any small 3‑power, g(c)=α rounded down to nearest 1/2025!. Compute α for each c by finding minimal N satisfying divisor‑sum condition (use powers of 3 for M, otherwise multiples of 6). Then sum m_c=⌊2025!·α⌋, reduce p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfall: ensure N<M for c=0, N>n/2, and handle c=4M (n=5M) where N may exceed M.

Insights:  
- For n‑Norwegian, smallest N = (n‑1)(1‑1/p) where p = smallest odd divisor of n‑1 (if n‑1 even, ignore 2; if n‑1 a power of 2 use p=4).  
- M=3^{2025!}. For any odd prime ≤2025, M≡1 (mod p); thus for c even, n‑1=M‑1+c ≡c (mod p) (except p=3 where n‑1≡c‑1).  
- Hence for each given c>0, p = smallest odd prime divisor of c (unless c≡1 mod 3, then p=3).  
- c=0 ⇒ p=5 (smallest odd divisor of M‑1).  
- c=4M ⇒ n‑1=5M‑1 ≡4 (mod p) for all p≤2025, so p>2025 (unknown).  
- For p≤2025, g(c)=1‑1/p (except c=0 gives 1‑1/5‑1/2025!).  
- For p>2025, g(c)=1‑ceil(2025!/p)/2025! = (2025!‑⌊2025!/p⌋‑1)/2025!.  

Compute p’s:  
c=0 →5; c=1848374→11; c=10162574→5081287 (>2025); c=265710644→29; c=44636594→17.  

Sum S = Σg = (6·2025! –[2025!/5+2025!/11+2025!/29+2025!/17+⌊2025!/5081287⌋+⌊2025!/p_big⌋+3])/2025!  

Need p_big = smallest odd prime factor of 5·3^{2025!}‑1. Find it, compute ⌊2025!/p_big⌋, then reduce S = p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991.  

Pitfalls: ensure p=3 case (c≡1 mod 3); handle c=0 extra –1/2025!; treat p=4 only if n‑1 is power of 2 (not here).

Insights: f(n) = min X with three distinct divisors summing to n. For large n, optimal X uses its two largest proper divisors: X + X/2 + X/3 ≥ n ⇒ X ≥ 6n/11. Actual ratios f(n)/n are the “best” fractions <2/3 (Farey sequence) – e.g. 6/11,4/7,3/5,8/13,… plus 2/3. For n = M + c (M=3^{2025!}), c≪M, the ratio is one of those fractions with small denominator (≤2025). Since 2025! is divisible by every denominator, g(c)=f(M+c)/M exactly. Compute each ratio for the six c’s, sum them, reduce, then output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure f uses three *distinct* divisors; verify that for huge M the same small‑denominator fractions apply; handle c=4M (n=5M) where ratio =2/3·5=10/3>1 (still a fraction). Use exact rational arithmetic.

Insights: f(n)=min N with three distinct divisors summing to n ⇒ N must be the largest divisor used. For given N, max sum of two other distinct divisors = s(N). To minimize N for a target n, use N with largest possible s(N).  
If N is multiple of 6, s(N)=N/2+N/3=5N/6, giving n≤(11/6)N ⇒ N≥6n/11. Smallest such N is 6·⌈n/11⌉. For huge n (≈M), any N not divisible by 6 has s(N)≤(3/4)N, so N+ s(N) ≤ (7/4)N > (11/6)N, forcing larger N. Thus for n≥~M the optimal N is exactly 6·⌈n/11⌉.  
Hence for each c, f(M+c)=6·⌈(M+c)/11⌉.  
Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f/M⌋/2025! = ⌊2025!·6·⌈(M+c)/11⌉/M⌋/2025!. Since M≫2025! and ⌈(M+c)/11⌉=⌈M/11⌉ (c negligible), the floor equals 2025!·6·⌈M/11⌉/M = 6·⌈M/11⌉/M·2025! which is exactly 6·⌈M/11⌉/M = 6/11 (M≡? mod 11). Because M=3^{2025!} mod 11 = 3^{2025! mod10} (φ(11)=10). 2025!≡0 (mod10) ⇒ M≡3^{0}=1 (mod11). So ⌈M/11⌉ = (M+10)/11. Hence f/M = 6·(M+10)/(11M)=6/11+60/(11M). The extra term <1/2025! so floor gives 6·(M+10)/11·2025!/M = 6·2025!/11 + tiny → g(c)=6/11 for all six c.  
Sum = 6·6/11 = 36/11 ⇒ p+q=36+11=47.  
Answer: 47 mod 99991 = 47.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. For huge n=3^K+δ (K≫1) the optimal triple is (d, n/3−d, n/3+d) where d|n/3, giving f≈2n/3. For n=3^K (δ=0) and n=5·3^K, exact f=2/3 n and 10/3 n. For small δ (≲10⁶) the same pattern holds; f/M = 2/3 + O(δ/M) with denominator a power of 3 ≤3^K. Since 2025! contains 3^1010 only, all fractions truncate to 2/3 (or 10/3 for 5M). Thus g(0)=g(4M)=2/3, g(5M)=10/3, and the other four c’s also give 2/3. Sum = 2/3+2/3+10/3+2/3+2/3+2/3 = 20/3 = p/q (reduced). p+q=20+3=23; 23 mod 99991 = 23.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Minimal ratio a/b occurs when a has two proper divisors summing to b−a. Small a give fractions: 6/11 (a multiple of 6, b=11a/6), 4/7 (a=4,b=7), 3/5 (a=6,b=10→3/5), 2/3 (a=6,b=9→2/3), etc. The smallest possible ratio is 6/11; any n divisible by 11 attains f(n)=6n/11 (optimal). For n not multiple of 11, next best ratio is 4/7 (if n≡0 mod 7), then 3/5 (if n≡0 mod 5), then 2/3 (if n≡0 mod 3), else larger fractions from a=8 (8/13), etc. Since M=3^{2025!} is a power of 3, M≡0 (mod 3) but not mod 5,7,11. Offsets c give N=M+c. Check divisibility: only N with c=0,4M,1848374,… may be multiples of 11,7,5,3. Compute which c make N divisible by 11,7,5,3. Then f(N)/M = corresponding ratio (6/11,4/7,3/5,2/3). g(c)=⌊2025!·f(N)/M⌋/2025! = that ratio (since 2025! divisible by denominators). Sum g(c)=Σ ratios. Reduce to p/q, compute (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure N’s divisibility by each denominator; for large c like 4M, N=5M divisible by 5 and 3, pick smallest ratio (2/3). Use smallest applicable ratio per N. Compute sum: e.g., if N divisible by 11 →6/11; else if by 7 →4/7; else if by 5 →3/5; else if by 3 →2/3. Then sum fractions, simplify, find p+q mod 99991.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)/n = min (L/S) where S|n and L/S is the best ratio for sum S. Global minima: 6/11 (S=11), 4/7 (7), 10/17 (17), 3/5 (10), 14/23 (23), 8/13 (13), … then 2/3 (S=9). Since M≡1 (mod any S coprime to 3), n=M+c ⇒ n≡c+1 (mod S). For each c, pick smallest‑ratio S dividing c+1; if none, use 2/3 (S=9). g(c)=f(n)/n (floor irrelevant as 2025! divisible by denominators). Values: g(0)=2/3; g(4M)=5·2/3=10/3; g(1848374)=16/25; g(10162574)=30/47; g(265710644)=64/97; g(44636594)=110/167. Sum =125561848/19033825 ⇒ (p+q) mod 99991 = 8687. Pitfalls: ensure M≡1 mod S (S∤3), handle S multiples of 3 (fallback 2/3), and that 2025! multiples all denominators.

Insights: f(n) = min c where ∃ distinct a,b|c, a+b+c=n.  For n≈M=3^{2025!} (huge) the optimal triple is (d, n/3−d, n/3+d) with d|n/3, giving f≈2n/3.  For n=M (c=0) and n=5M (c=4M) exact f=2/3 M and 10/3 M.  For all other c (≤10⁶) the same pattern holds, so g(c)=⌊2025!·f/M⌋/2025! = 2/3 (or 10/3 for 5M).  Sum = 20/3 ⇒ p+q=23 ⇒ answer 23 (mod 99991).

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)/n = min L/s over s|n, where L is minimal lcm for sum s. Global minima: ratios in increasing order → 6/11 (s≡0 mod 11), 4/7 (7‑mult), 10/17, 14/23, 8/13, 18/29, 12/19, 16/25, 20/31,… For each n=M+c compute smallest s (by this order) dividing n. M=3^{2025!}; for s coprime to 3, M≡1 (mod s). For s with 3‑factor, M≡0 (mod 3^k) and ≡1 (mod t). Use CRT. Then g(c)=⌊2025!·(L/s)⌋/2025! = L/s (denominator divides 2025!). Sum six g(c) → rational p/q; compute (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: assume M≡1 for all s (wrong for multiples of 3); need correct M mod s via CRT. Use ordered ratio list to find minimal s for each c.

Insights: f(n)=min c where ∃ distinct proper divisors a,b of c with a+b=n−c. So g(c)=⌊2025!·c/M⌋/2025!. For M=3^{2025!}, c values are 0,5M, and small offsets ≡2 (mod 3). For huge M, the minimal c is ≈⌊2n/3⌋; if n≡0 (mod 3) it equals (2/3)n exactly. For n≡2 (mod 3) the minimal c equals (2/3)n−Δ where Δ depends only on n mod 9 (periodic). Compute Δ for each offset using small‑K experiments (K≥19) where M>max offset; pattern stabilizes: Δ=0 for n≡0, Δ= M/3·(1−(n mod 9)/3). Then g(c)=c/M (exact, denominator divides 2025!). Sum the six fractions, reduce, compute (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure c≠a,b, use distinct divisors; floor matters only when denominator exceeds 3^{1010}. Use 2025! factorization to truncate high‑power‑3 parts.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Factor out common divisor g|n: f(n)=g·f₀(n/g) where f₀ is for coprime triples. For n=M+c (M=3^N), v₃(n)=0 for c≡2 (mod 3) → g=1, so f(n)=f₀(n). For c=0,4M, g=3^N (or 3^{N‑1}) → f known = (2/3)n. Compute f₀ for the six n (c values) via brute‑force for modest N (≥18) since only low‑order base‑3 digits matter; denominators are powers of 3 ≤3^{18} dividing 2025!. Then S=∑f(M+c)/M = (∑f_i)/M. Let v=v₃(∑f_i); p=∑f_i/3^v, q=3^{N‑v}. Compute p+q mod 99991 using fast exponentiation (N=2025!). Pitfalls: ensure f₀ computed correctly (triples distinct), handle large exponents modulo 99991, verify denominators divide 2025! so floor in g(c) is exact.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Minimal ratio L/n is achieved by “base” sums S whose optimal triple has LCM=S·p/q (p/q in lowest terms). Base S (sorted by p/q): 11→6/11, 7→4/7, 17→10/17, 10→3/5, 23→14/23, 13→8/13, 29→20/29, 16→5/8, 19→12/19, 41→26/41, 47→30/47, 25→16/25, 53→42/53, 59→46/59, 31→20/31, 71→44/71, 37→22/37, 83→48/83, 43→26/43, 89→54/89, 97→64/97, 167→110/167,…  

M=3^{2025!} ⇒ M≡1 (mod S) for any S coprime to 3. For n=M+c (c≪M) we have n≡c+1 (mod S). The smallest base S dividing c+1 gives the minimal ratio r.  

c values:  
c=0 → no base S divides 1 ⇒ use S=9 (ratio 2/3).  
c=4M ⇒ n=5M, still divisible by 9 ⇒ ratio 2/3, multiplied by 5 ⇒ g=10/3.  
c+1=1848375 ⇒ smallest base divisor 25 ⇒ r=16/25.  
c+1=10162575 ⇒ divisor 47 ⇒ r=30/47.  
c+1=265710645 ⇒ divisor 97 ⇒ r=64/97.  
c+1=44636595 ⇒ divisor 167 ⇒ r=110/167.  

Since 2025! is divisible by all denominators, floor does not change values: g(c)=r (or 5r for 4M).  

Sum = 2/3 + 10/3 + 16/25 + 30/47 + 64/97 + 110/167 = 125561848/19033825.  

p+q mod 99991 = 8687.   (Pitfalls: ensure M≡1 mod S, include S=9 for powers of 3, use base‑S list, not miss larger S with better ratios.)

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Minimal LCM/sum ratios come from primitive triples: (2,3,6) → 6/11, (1,2,4) → 4/7, (2,5,10) → 10/17, (1,3,6) → 3/5, (1,4,8) → 8/13,… Increasing ratios. For n=M+ c (M=3^{2025!}), M≡1 (mod s) for s∤3, so n divisible only by sums s that divide c (or by powers of 3). Check c’s:  
c=0,4M → smallest divisor s=9 (ratio 2/3). For 4M factor 5 multiplies ratio → 10/3.  
c=1848374 → smallest divisor s=25 (ratio 16/25).  
c=10162574 → s=47 (30/47).  
c=265710644 → s=97 (64/97).  
c=44636594 → s=167 (110/167).  
Thus g’s: 2/3, 10/3, 16/25, 30/47, 64/97, 110/167. Sum = 125561848/19033825 → p+q≡8687 (mod 99991). Pitfalls: c=4M multiplies ratio; ensure s divides n, not just M. Use primitive‑sum list ordered by ratio.
